h1: Grape ale, the Italian hybrid style
title: Grape Ale: The Italian Hybrid Style | Craft Beer School
desc: What grape ale is, how Italian brewers blend grape must with malt and what to taste for in a glass that sits between beer and wine.
teaser: Half the glass is beer, half behaves like wine. Grape ale is the style where Italian brewers stopped choosing.
standfirst: Grape ale is beer brewed with grapes or grape must in the fermenter. Italy made it a style of its own. Here is how it is made, what it tastes like and how to judge one.
sections: Grape ale is a beer that borrows a vineyard

Grape ale starts as an ordinary malt wort, usually pale, then picks up grapes, grape must or unfermented grape juice before or during fermentation. The grapes add sugar, acid, tannin and the aromatics of the variety. The malt still carries the body. The result is a beer that can smell like a white wine and finish like a Belgian ale.

Italian craft brewers built the style in the 2000s, which made sense in a country with a vineyard in nearly every region. The BJCP style guidelines now list Grape Ale under fruit beers, with the Italian version as the reference point. Most examples land roughly between 5% and 10% ABV.
The grape decides more than the malt does

The variety matters more than the base beer. A white aromatic grape such as Moscato or Malvasia gives floral, peachy notes. A red grape fermented on its skins adds colour, a little tannin and berry fruit. Brewers who use must or skins in the fermenter often call their beer by the grape name, the way a winemaker would.

The share of grape varies a great deal. Some brewers add a small dose of juice for aroma. Others make the grape a large share of the fermentables, which pushes the beer towards wine in body and acidity. Hops stay in the background. Bitterness is usually low because hop bitterness and wine-like acidity together taste harsh.
How a brewer actually adds the grapes

There are three common routes. Fresh crushed grapes or must go into the fermenter with the wort, so both ferment together. Grape juice is added later, after primary fermentation slows, which keeps more fresh fruit aroma. Or the brewer ferments the grape must separately with a wine yeast and blends it into finished beer.

Each route changes the beer. Co-fermentation gives the most integrated flavour but less control. Late additions taste brighter and fruitier. Blending gives the brewer the most control over acidity. Some Italian grape ales then spend months in oak barrels, which is where the wine side really comes forward.

Grapes also bring wild yeast and bacteria on their skins. Some brewers welcome that for a tart, rustic beer. Others sulphite or pasteurise the must first so their chosen yeast does the work.
What to look for in the glass

Pour it into a wine glass or a tulip. Colour runs from pale straw to deep ruby depending on the grape. Carbonation is usually lively, closer to a sparkling wine than to a pale lager. On the nose look for the grape first: stone fruit and flowers from white varieties, red berries and a little earthiness from red ones. The malt sits underneath as a light bready note.

On the palate a good grape ale is dry, with clear acidity and a short, clean finish. Watch for faults. Vinegar sharpness points to acetic bacteria. Excess sulphur can come from the grapes or from a stressed yeast. A cloying, sweet finish usually means fermentation stopped early. If these off notes are new to you, our guide to beer off flavours walks through each one.
Grape ale in an Indian glass

India has the grapes. Nashik grows Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc and Shiraz for wine. The Bangalore Blue grape around Bengaluru has a grapey, foxy aroma that tastes nothing like a European wine grape and could make a very local beer. A brewpub with access to fresh must at harvest, roughly January to April in Maharashtra, could brew a seasonal batch that no import can match.

Heat is the risk. Fresh grapes and must spoil fast in a warm brewery. A co-fermentation at 25 °C or more throws harsh fusel alcohol. Keep the must cold and the fermentation in the low 20s °C. Indian food helps too: a dry, tart white grape ale cuts through a rich paneer tikka or a Goan prawn curry in a way a heavy stout cannot.
Tasting it next to its neighbours

The best way to learn grape ale is to taste it beside the styles it borrows from. Set out a pale ale, a dry white wine and a grape ale, small pours of 50 ml each, with water and something to eat. Notice where the grape ale shares the wine's acidity and where it keeps the beer's malt and bubbles. Compare it with a familiar pale ale to see how little the hops are doing.

Doing that well takes a trained palate, a shared vocabulary for aroma and a habit of writing down what you find. Most drinkers can say they like a beer. Fewer can say why it tastes the way it does, which is the gap structured sensory training fills.

Find one grape ale, Italian if you can, or any beer brewed with grape must. Pour it beside a white wine made from the same or a similar grape. Write down three aromas from each before you taste. Then look for the grape in the beer. If you can pick it out on the nose without looking at the label, you are already tasting like a judge.
faqs: Is grape ale a beer or a wine?
It is a beer. The base is a malt wort fermented with yeast. Grapes or grape must are added as a fruit. In flavour it often sits close to a sparkling wine.
Where does grape ale come from?
Italian craft brewers developed it in the 2000s. The BJCP guidelines now list Grape Ale as a fruit beer style, with Italian examples as the reference.
Most examples sit between roughly 5% and 10% ABV, depending on how much grape sugar the brewer adds.
What food goes with grape ale?
Dry, tart grape ales suit rich dishes with cream, butter or seafood, such as paneer tikka or a coconut prawn curry. Treat pairings as suggestions to try, not rules.
